newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Air of normality obscures conflict in Algeria.
newsitem.headline: Air of normality obscures conflict in Algeria.

text.p: Nearly a year after the election of former general Liamine Zeroual as president on promises to restore security, central Algiers with its teeming coffee shops and well-stocked businesses displays an air of normality.
Relaxed policemen on a roadblock near Algiers' town hall, 700 metres (yards) from the Casbah, seem to underline confidence in the security situation in the Algerian capital.

"We feel secure here but going more than 60 km (40 miles) outside Algiers, could be a different story," said Houria, fiancee of a newly wealthy young businessman, at a table for dinner with seven friends in an expensive restaurant.
But her friend Dalila whispered that many of the men in the restaurant could be armed. Three young civilians, outside scrutinising the street, betrayed the sense of normality inside.

"If we compare ourselves to what many other villages and towns are going through, we can say we are lucky. But I'm still waiting for telecommunications workers to come to fix my telephone at home in the Casbah.
"They have not shown up for several months because they apparently fear attacks," said Mohamed as he left a post office in his latest attempt to get it repaired.
Many residents appear a world apart from the government which is campaigning to get support for a November 28 referendum to change the constitution.
Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia and ministers are travelling the country presenting the referendum as a way to ensure stability and development before a general election next year.

But most residents at one gathering in violence-stricken Baraki, near Algiers, assailed Ouyahia with questions and claims over jobs, housing and compensation for family members killed and property destroyed by Moslem guerrillas.

"Of the 25 people who spoke in the meeting chaired by Ouyahia, no one pronounced the word constitution or election. This at least shows where the gap between the citizens and the authorities is on the ground," said one local journalist.
Official media quoted Ouyahia as saying: "Contrary to what some circles state, Baraki's population do not reject the constitution draft."
The scene, repeated in similar meetings, suggests an uphill struggle for the government to draw support for the vote as opposition leaders urge a "no" vote or boycott.

"The turnout rate should be the lowest. If you vote in this constitution, you will harm yourselves. The (authorities') ballots are machines converting every vote into yes," said secular opposition leader Said Saadi in a campaign rally in the coastal town of Cherchell, seat of the army's main academy.
"The only reason they draft such a constitution proves the authorities have no confidence in the people," he added.

Hardline anti-Islamists, like Saadi, as well as legal moderate Islamists, who supported last year's presidential ballot and gained more than one third of the votes, are turning against the authorities this time.

"This draft constitution limits the freedoms, repudiates democracy and gives, like the previous constitution, the president the powers to rule like emperor," said Mohamed Dane, leader of legal Islamist Hamas.
Hamas is seen as an indirect supporter of the government with two of its members as ministers in the cabinet.

"With 100,000 dead, it is a war which discloses the lie about the 'last quarter hour'," said Djamel Zenati of the Socialist Forces Front, the main secular party campaigning for a "no" vote. He was referring to the authorities' claims that Moslem fundamentalists, blamed for conflict in which more than 50,000 have died, were near defeat.

"It is the peace which is residual not the terrorism," he said. The day he was speaking, a car bomb ripped through a bus near Algiers, killing 10 people and wounding 20, according to the official toll.
"There were more than 100 casualties, including at least 20 dead," said one resident who witnessed the explosion.
State-run television, urging viewers to keep children away from the "image of horror", showed limbs scattered, wounded screaming, and a rescuer picking up a foot and part of leg.
